title: After the last page
hookLine: the Tanakh closes, and Jewish history goes on
carry: the pages ran out; the handing-on didn't

lines: A PEOPLE WAKES UP THE NEXT DAY.
cards: Close a Tanakh and look at the last printed page. A few days ago we heard its final words: Cyrus's call to the exiles, let him go up. Then white space.
And yet the people in that book did not stop on that page. Somebody went up.
Somebody rebuilt a wall, planted a vineyard, argued with a neighbor, married, buried a parent, taught a child to read the very scroll that had just run out of pages. A book can end.
A people keeps waking up the next morning. Today we step off the last page into the long stretch of Jewish life the Bible itself never narrates.

teach.b: The Talmud, in tractate Bava Batra, lays out an order: the Prophets close with the Twelve, the short books like Malachi, and the Writings close with Chronicles.
So the Tanakh has more than one ending, and each one leans forward. Malachi's last lines tell the people to remember the teaching of Moses, then make a promise.

teach.h: I WILL SEND YOU ELIJAH THE PROPHET.
teach.b: In the King James words: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD." The Prophets end with someone still on the way.
At Passover, some families pour a cup for Elijah and open the door. Then a harder turn.
The Talmud, in tractate Yoma, says that when the last prophets, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, died, the holy spirit of prophecy departed from Israel.
But the same passage adds that people still heard a bat kol, an echo of a heavenly voice. Quieter, but not silence. So who carries the story now?

The opening of Pirkei Avot answers with a chain. Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly.

teach.h: A CHAIN OF HANDS: RAISE UP STUDENTS.
teach.b: They gave three pieces of advice: be careful in judgment, raise up many students, and build a fence around the Torah. When the prophets go quiet, the answer is students.

how: Jews read and study the Tanakh alongside the teachings of the rabbis who came after it, and some communities study Pirkei Avot, which opens with the chain of tradition from Moses, on Sabbath afternoons in the weeks after Passover.

o: a prophet's daughter who carried on his work
a bell rung in the Temple to call people in
an echo of a heavenly voice, heard after prophecy

s: when prophecy went quiet, Jewish tradition says nothing was heard at all
the Talmud says the holy spirit of prophecy departed, but people still heard a bat kol, an echo of a heavenly voice.
the Prophets section ends looking forward to Elijah
Malachi's last lines promise that Elijah the prophet will be sent.
Pirkei Avot's chain stops with the prophets
the prophets hand the Torah on to the men of the Great Assembly, who say: raise up many students.

games.q: you live just after the last prophets. there are no new prophets now. what does the tradition say comes next?
o: wait for a new prophet before doing anything.
close the books; the story is over.
raise up many students and keep teaching.
games.why: Pirkei Avot's chain passes the Torah from the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly, and one of their three sayings is to raise up many students.

practice: Bring to mind one ending in your own life, a graduation, a move, a funeral, a last day at a job, something that looked like the last page.
Now look at the first ordinary morning after: who handed you something, or whom did you hand something to? If you pray, give thanks in words from your tradition for what continued.

wordCard.voice: Bat kol. An echo of a heavenly voice, still heard, the Talmud says, after the Tanakh closed and prophecy went quiet. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: an echo of a heavenly voice, which the Talmud says was still heard after prophecy ceased.
